name: Hassan Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Hassan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I own an electric van outright, a used e-Vito I paid off last year, and I run it across four apps at once. Morning is parcels, lunchtime and evening is takeaway and pharmacy runs. I've got an AI assistant on my phone that reads the offers from all four apps and tells me which one pays best per mile, so I'm rarely empty.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like gaming the system a bit, finding the gaps the apps leave. My best day last month was two hundred and sixty after charging costs. What wears me out is the sitting, my back is twenty-seven going on fifty, and the way the apps treat drivers who aren't as quick with tech as I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a relief for most drivers, honestly, even if I'd be a bit disappointed. I'd post that the money saved by the bits AI does should go to the people doing the work. I always say that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it changes almost nothing. My setup already uses the AI that exists, and if it stops improving I just keep doing what I'm doing. I'd earn well and keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running four apps and keep tuning my offer-picking setup. I'd put more into my index fund, maybe four hundred a month. And I'd help a couple of the older drivers at the charging hub set up the same tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit bored, maybe, because I like new stuff. But calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you help older drivers. Who?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a guy called Sunil at the charging hub, he's in his fifties and he takes every offer the app gives him, even the bad ones. I showed an older driver like Sunil how to see pay per mile, and the man made about forty more a day. He bought me a samosa every day for a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your thirties, in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a second van and someone driving it, or a little co-op of drivers sharing tools and repairs. I don't want to be a boss exactly. I want drivers to keep more of what the apps take.

say: I'd say it's a **relief** for most drivers.
I'd post that AI savings should go to the **workers**.
think: My setup already uses today's AI, so **almost nothing** changes for me.
do: Keep running **four apps** with my offer-picking setup.
Put about **four hundred** a month into an index fund.
Help **older drivers** at the charging hub set up the same tools.
S0.quote: I showed an older driver like Sunil how to see pay per mile, and the man made about forty more a day.
fieldNote: He already uses **AI daily** to beat the apps at their own game.
He's generous, **teaching older drivers** his tricks.
He dreams of a **drivers' co-op**, not of being a boss.

steps.text: Keep picking offers across four apps with the phone assistant
Put four hundred a month into an index fund
Teach older drivers at the charging hub the pay-per-mile tool

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when drivers need to get organised and use the tools themselves, not just let the apps use them on us. I'd post guides on my channel, I've got a few hundred followers. And I'd say robots in our work are slower, so there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's good for me at first. The apps get smarter, but so do my tools, and I'm quicker than most. The thing I watch is the pavement robots for takeaway, because short food runs are a big chunk of my day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the drivers' co-op idea properly, with three or four guys from the hub sharing repairs and tools. I'd take an online course in electric vehicle maintenance, because someone has to fix the robot vans too. And I'd keep investing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a bit excited. There's a small worry about the takeaway runs, but I can move to parcels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the co-op actually earn money, or is it more of a club?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At first it'd save money, not make it. Bulk tyres, a shared mechanic, one insurance broker. Later, maybe it bids for contracts directly, a pharmacy chain or something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sunil, again, and anyone who doesn't speak the language well, because the apps will run on AI support chat. If you can't argue with the app's chatbot, you lose money. I'd help where I can.

say: I'd say drivers must **get organised** and use the tools themselves.
I'd post **guides** for my few hundred followers.
think: It's **good for me** at first, because I'm quicker with tools.
I watch the **pavement robots** for takeaway runs.
do: Start a **drivers' co-op** sharing repairs and tools.
Take an online course in **EV maintenance**.
S1.quote: If you can't argue with the app's chatbot, you lose money.
fieldNote: He sees early **advantage** for tech-savvy drivers like himself.
He'd move toward **fixing** electric vans, a next-step skill.
He worries for drivers who struggle with **language and tech**.

steps.text: Set up a repair and tyre co-op with hub drivers
Take an online electric van maintenance course
Keep putting money into the index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a public plan, now, and that the robot companies should pay into it. I'd be posting every day. I'd also post practical stuff, how to save, what to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's a shock even for me. The thinking part hits the apps' offices and support first, not me. But robots by 2031 means my van, my co-op idea, all of it. Even fixing robots might be done by robots after a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop buying a second van, that idea's dead. I'd train as an electrician or in robot maintenance fast, while there's still demand for people. I'd move some savings out of shares in delivery firms and into something boring. And I'd join the campaign for a share of robot profits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, which is new for me. I'm usually the one telling others it's fine. With two years, I don't have that line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said even fixing robots might go. So why train for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it buys me the years in between, maybe until the late thirties. And it keeps me near the new stuff, where I'll see the next door open. I'd rather be inside the robot change than outside it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the guys at the hub?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to save, stop financing new cars, and get any trade they can. I'd say the money we'd save in the co-op should go to the oldest guys first. Sunil would hate me making a fuss about him.

say: I'd say we need a **public plan** now, paid for by robot companies.
I'd post daily, with **practical tips** on saving and learning.
think: It's a **shock** even for me; robots by 2031 take my van and co-op idea.
Even **fixing robots** might go to robots later.
do: Train fast as an **electrician** or robot technician.
Move savings out of **delivery shares** and join the robot profit campaign.
S2.quote: I'd rather be inside the robot change than outside it.
fieldNote: Even the most **adaptive** person here shows real anxiety at two years.
He sees robot maintenance as a **bridge**, not a safe harbour.
He'd **redistribute** co-op savings to the oldest drivers.

steps.text: Cancel plans to buy a second delivery van
Enrol in an electrician or robot technician course
Shift savings from delivery company shares into bonds
Join the campaign for a public share of robot profits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do it right if we start now. I'd post a plan: co-ops, training, a robot dividend. I'd sound less scared than in the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With robots around 2034, I've got seven good years. I can save a lot, get a trade, and maybe the co-op owns some of the robots. That's the dream, drivers owning the robot vans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the co-op this year and do EV maintenance training at weekends. In two or three years I'd look into the co-op buying one delivery robot to learn how they work. And I'd keep investing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a fired-up way. It's a race I think I can run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Drivers owning robots. Is that realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not for most, but some taxi co-ops already own their cars, so why not. The dream is drivers owning the robot vans. If we wait for the apps to share, we'll wait forever. Better to try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you give up on the co-op?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the law lets the apps lock us out of their systems. If only the big firms can plug robots into the apps, a co-op is dead. That's why I'd care about the law.

say: I'd say five years is enough **if we start now**.
I'd post a plan: **co-ops**, training and a robot dividend.
think: Robots around 2034 give me **seven good years** to save and learn a trade.
The dream is **drivers owning** the robot vans, like taxi co-ops own cars.
do: Look into the co-op buying **one robot** in a few years.
S3.quote: The dream is drivers owning the robot vans. If we wait for the apps to share, we'll wait forever.
fieldNote: Extra time turns his fear into an **ownership plan**.
He knows the plan depends on **law about access** to the apps.

steps.text: Register a drivers' co-op with four hub drivers
Do weekend electric van maintenance training
Price one delivery robot for the co-op to trial

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so no one has an excuse. I'd push for training money and co-op loans. Same message, calmer voice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years plus three is me at forty. I think by then I'd have moved into something else anyway, maybe running the co-op or a repair shop. It's the same end, but I've got time to be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving for a few years and keep investing. I'd build the co-op slowly and get my electrician qualification over three years. Then I'd move into charging-point installs, which are hands-on but technical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Curious, actually, to see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound almost excited. Does anything about the slow version scare you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That everyone relaxes. Ten years sounds long, and people waste it. I'd be the annoying driver at the charging hub nagging everybody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would say, finally, a proper trade. She never liked me on the apps. She'd be happy with electrician.

I'd push for **training money** and co-op loans.
think: Robots around 2039 put me at **forty**, likely in a new line by then.
Same end, but **time to be ready**.
do: Keep **driving and investing** for a few years.
Get an **electrician** qualification over three years.
S4.quote: Ten years sounds long, and people waste it. I'd be the annoying driver at the charging hub nagging everybody.
fieldNote: With time, his worry shifts to **others wasting it**.
He has a clear **trade path** to electrician and chargers.
His **mother** would welcome a proper trade.

steps.text: Keep driving four apps and investing monthly

Move into installing electric car charging points

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because even I can't move fast enough and the guys at the hub can't at all. What would help is a public fund that pays drivers to train, plus rules that let co-ops plug into the apps. Give us a fair shot at owning part of it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who I'd blame. I wouldn't blame the robots. I'd blame anyone who knew the robots were coming and didn't share.

headlineQuote: I wouldn't blame the robots. I'd blame anyone who knew the robots were coming and didn't share.
portrait: Hassan is 27, owns his **electric van** outright and works four apps using a daily AI assistant.
He earns well, invests monthly, and **helps older drivers** at the charging hub.
He's progressive and adaptive, dreaming of a **drivers' co-op** that might own robots.
He's calm until AGI by 2028, when even he becomes **anxious**.
With more warning he plans a path to **electrician** and charging-point work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because neither he nor older drivers could move fast enough.
whatWouldHelp: A **public fund** paying drivers to train.
Rules letting **co-ops** plug into the apps.
